From interactive whiteboards to artificial intelligence-powered learning devices, technology is reshaping classroom experiences, improving lesson delivery, encouraging student participation and expanding access to educational resources across schools, writes GODWIN AIKIGBE The traditional classroom is undergoing a transformation as digital technology introduces new ways of teaching, learning and sharing knowledge. Teachers are increasingly using electronic devices to explain complex subjects, assess students’ understanding and make lessons more engaging. Smart gadgets can help students visualise scientific processes, explore digital libraries, practise mathematical problems and collaborate on assignments. They also provide teachers with tools for preparing lessons, monitoring academic progress and adapting instruction to different learning needs. Although the availability of these devices varies across schools, their growing use highlights the potential of technology to improve educational outcomes when supported by reliable infrastructure, appropriate training and effective teaching methods. Here are 10 gadgets transforming classroom learning. Tablets Tablets are among the most versatile devices used in modern classrooms. Their portability, touchscreen interfaces and ability to run educational applications make them suitable for pupils across different age groups. Students can use tablets to read electronic textbooks, watch instructional videos, complete assignments, solve mathematical problems and access digital dictionaries. Teachers can also distribute learning materials electronically, administer quizzes and provide feedback. Unlike conventional textbooks, tablets can accommodate numerous educational resources in a single device. Students can revisit recorded lessons and practise difficult topics at their own pace. Tablets can also support learners with special educational needs through applications featuring text-to-speech, speech-to-text, adjustable fonts and other accessibility functions. However, schools must establish clear usage guidelines to minimise distractions from games, social media and unrelated online content. Devices should be selected according to curriculum requirements, durability, affordability and the availability of suitable educational applications. Laptops, notebook computers Laptops provide students and teachers with computing capabilities that support research, writing, data analysis, presentations and digital content creation. Students can use them to prepare assignments, organise research findings, develop spreadsheets, create presentations and learn programming. These activities develop practical digital skills that are valuable in higher education and the workplace. For teachers, laptops make it easier to prepare lesson notes, create assessment materials, maintain academic records and organise teaching resources. They can also support virtual lessons and access to online professional development programmes. In science and technology subjects, students can use specialised software to conduct simulations, analyse information and explore concepts that might otherwise require expensive laboratory equipment. Laptops are particularly valuable for secondary schools and tertiary institutions, where students are expected to undertake more independent research and complete complex assignments. Nevertheless, their effectiveness depends on regular maintenance, software updates, reliable power supply and adequate training for teachers and students. Interactive whiteboards Interactive whiteboards allow teachers to display and manipulate digital content on large classroom screens. Depending on the model, teachers and students can write, draw, annotate diagrams and interact directly with displayed materials. The devices make lessons more visual and participatory. A science teacher, for instance, can display an animated illustration of the human heart, while a mathematics teacher can demonstrate geometric shapes and transformations. Geography lessons can benefit from interactive maps, satellite images and visual representations of weather patterns. Language teachers can display passages, highlight grammatical structures and use multimedia resources to support comprehension. Interactive whiteboards also enable teachers to combine text, photographs, audio and video in a single lesson. This can help explain concepts that are difficult to communicate through spoken explanations alone. For schools investing in the technology, however, installation costs, electricity requirements, maintenance and teacher training must be considered. The equipment delivers the greatest value when it supports active learning rather than simply replacing a conventional chalkboard with a digital display. Digital projectors Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. They are useful for presentations, documentary clips, instructional videos, diagrams, maps and examination preparation. Teachers can use them to demonstrate practical procedures, compare images and explain complicated processes. For example, a biology teacher can project an enlarged image of a plant cell, helping students identify its structures. A history teacher can display photographs of historical events, monuments and personalities to provide visual context for a lesson. Projectors can also support group presentations, enabling students to communicate research findings to their classmates. Compared with interactive whiteboards, conventional projectors may offer schools a more affordable way to introduce digital visual learning, particularly where several classrooms can share the equipment. Their limitations include the need for suitable projection surfaces, adequate lighting conditions and compatible computers or other devices. Regular servicing and access to electricity are also necessary. Smart televisions Smart televisions bring internet-connected audiovisual learning into classrooms. Depending on their capabilities, they can display educational videos, documentaries, presentations and content from approved online learning platforms. They are especially useful for lessons involving visual demonstrations, language instruction, environmental education and scientific processes. For instance, students studying climate change can watch educational documentaries explaining rising temperatures, extreme weather and environmental conservation. Language learners can watch instructional videos that demonstrate pronunciation, listening comprehension and conversational skills. Smart televisions can also support recorded lessons, allowing teachers to revisit explanations or introduce students to specialist knowledge beyond the school’s immediate resources. In schools with limited access to individual devices, a shared smart television can provide an entry point into digital education by allowing an entire class to benefit from the same content. However, teachers must select reliable, age-appropriate materials and avoid allowing entertainment content to distract students from lesson objectives. Internet access, screen positioning and sound quality should also be considered when planning classroom use. Smartphones Smartphones can become useful learning tools when schools establish appropriate rules for their use. Their portability and broad range of applications allow students to access electronic dictionaries, educational videos, revision questions, calculators and digital libraries. Teachers can also use them to communicate assignments, share announcements and provide additional learning resources. Students preparing for examinations can use approved applications to practise questions, review definitions and revisit difficult topics outside classroom hours. Smartphones can also support fieldwork. Students studying environmental science, for example, can take photographs, record observations and document changes in their surroundings for subsequent classroom discussions. Unsupervised internet access may also expose students to inappropriate content, cyberbullying and misinformation. Schools should therefore establish clear policies covering when phones may be used, which applications are permitted and how online activities should be supervised. Where personal devices create significant distractions, school-managed tablets or shared digital equipment may be more appropriate. Document cameras Document cameras allow teachers to project physical objects, printed pages, diagrams, handwritten notes and demonstrations onto a large screen. They are particularly useful when students need to observe details that may be difficult to see from their seats. A teacher can place a textbook beneath the camera to examine a diagram, demonstrate a mathematical calculation or explain how to complete an assignment. In science lessons, the camera can display specimens, leaves, minerals and other small objects for the entire class to observe. Document cameras can also support art lessons by showing drawing techniques, handwriting exercises and step-by-step demonstrations. Unlike conventional projectors, which generally display content from a connected computer or other media source, document cameras are designed to capture and enlarge physical materials in real time. They can therefore help schools combine traditional teaching resources with digital presentation methods without requiring every lesson to be fully computer-based. Digital microscopes Digital microscopes combine magnification with electronic imaging, allowing students to examine small objects and display their images on a computer, tablet or classroom screen. They can improve practical learning in biology, agricultural science, environmental studies and other scientific subjects. Students can observe the structure of plant tissues, examine insects, study prepared slides and investigate materials that are not easily visible to the naked eye. The ability to display magnified images to an entire class encourages group discussion. Teachers can guide students through observations while explaining the structures and processes they are examining. Some digital microscopes can capture photographs or videos, enabling students to document experiments and compare observations over time. The equipment can also support collaborative investigations, helping learners develop scientific observation, recording and analytical skills. However, digital microscopes should complement, rather than eliminate, hands-on laboratory activities. Schools must provide suitable specimens, basic laboratory materials, proper handling instructions and teacher supervision to ensure meaningful learning. Educational robotics kits Educational robotics kits introduce students to programming, engineering, logical reasoning and problem-solving through practical activities. Depending on the kit, students can assemble simple machines, programme movements, connect sensors and investigate how electronic components interact. For example, learners may build a small robot that follows a marked path, detects obstacles or responds to light. Such projects encourage students to test ideas, identify errors and improve their designs. Robotics activities can also introduce fundamental concepts in mathematics and science, including measurement, motion, energy, sequencing and cause-and-effect relationships. For older students, programmable microcontrollers and related learning devices can provide an introduction to electronics, automation and the principles underlying modern technologies. These activities help move learning beyond memorising definitions by giving students opportunities to apply theoretical knowledge to practical challenges. However, robotics kits can be expensive, and their benefits depend on the availability of trained teachers and suitable learning materials. Schools can reduce costs by sharing kits among groups, introducing low-cost programming platforms and organising practical sessions around specific curriculum objectives. AI-powered learning tools Artificial intelligence is introducing new capabilities into digital education through applications that provide personalised exercises, conversational assistance, automated feedback and adaptive learning experiences. AI-enabled tools can help students practise languages, explore unfamiliar concepts, generate revision questions and receive alternative explanations when they struggle with a subject. Teachers can also use approved AI applications to prepare lesson outlines, develop quizzes, adapt reading materials and identify topics requiring additional classroom attention. Some platforms analyse students’ responses to recommend exercises based on their performance. Such features can help teachers recognise learning gaps and provide more targeted support. However, AI-powered tools require careful supervision. They can generate inaccurate information, reflect biases or encourage students to rely on automated answers instead of developing independent reasoning skills. Schools should teach students to verify information, protect personal data and use AI responsibly. Teachers must also ensure that assignments and assessments measure genuine understanding rather than the ability to obtain answers from digital tools. AI should serve as an assistant to teachers and learners, not as a replacement for human guidance, professional judgement and meaningful classroom interaction. Conclusion The growing availability of educational gadgets offers schools opportunities to improve teaching, but purchasing equipment alone does not guarantee better academic performance. Schools must identify their learning needs, select suitable devices and train teachers to integrate technology into lesson plans. They should also budget for electricity, connectivity, repairs, software updates and eventual equipment replacement. In Nigeria, unequal access to electricity, internet services and affordable devices remains a significant challenge. Public-private partnerships, subsidised connectivity, shared device programmes and offline educational resources could help extend digital learning to underserved communities. Parents also have a role in encouraging responsible device use at home, while education authorities should establish standards for child protection, data privacy and the selection of educational applications. Most importantly, schools should regularly evaluate whether their technology investments are improving students’ understanding, participation and academic progress. Smart devices are most effective when they complement skilled teachers, sound curricula and practical learning experiences. With appropriate planning and equitable access, these gadgets can help create classrooms that are more engaging, interactive and responsive to the needs of today’s learners. Godwin Aikigbe
